To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) recurrent neural networks (RBNs) trained by a gradient ascent in Riemannian metrics are able to learn a variety of complex structures, such as the distantXOR problem, that are beyond the capabilities of HMMs; and (2) Riemannian training is an algorithm that does not depend on the choice of the network structure, the encoding of parameters, or the initial parameters.

1) the Riemannian geometry of neural networks can be used to derive a training procedure for recurrent neural networks that does not require back-propagation through time, and is therefore much more efficient; 2) this training procedure can be applied to networks with a sparse random architecture and random initial weights; 3) this procedure is able to train recurrent neural networks to solve a variety of tasks that cannot be solved by hidden Markov models.

(i) the Riemannian metrics introduced for feedforward networks in our companion paper can be extended to recurrent networks; (ii) the resulting gradient ascent algorithm is effective at learning a variety of sequential models, including complex structures such as intersections of multiple independent dependencies; (iii) this algorithm is effective on a wide variety of architectures and initial parameters; and (iv) the algorithm has a computational complexity comparable to backpropagation, even for networks with sparsely connected layers.

RNNs can indeed be trained to represent such complex data structures, but this requires a careful choice of architecture and learning algorithm, as well as a good initialization and a good training procedure, and that the Riemannian training method we propose here is well suited for this purpose.
